name: Prettyboymaxxing

lead: Prettyboymaxxing is the practice of optimising for a softer, prettier, more androgynous male look rather than a rugged, heavily masculine one. In forum usage it usually means a lean body, smooth clear skin, longer or carefully styled hair, a clean shave and a friendly-looking face.

The pitch from its supporters is that this look reads as approachable and is popular with younger audiences and on social media, and that most of its ingredients are reachable through grooming rather than surgery. Members post before-and-after threads to show what changed. No studies have tested the approach as a whole.

paras: Practitioners combine several low-intensity steps: leaning down to a lower body-fat level, a skincare routine aimed at even, clear skin, a haircut or longer style that frames the face, shaving, dropping glasses, and clothing choices. Posters describe these as the same areas covered by skinmaxxing, leanmaxxing, hairmaxxing and fashionmaxxing. One progress thread described changes over about eleven months.

The look itself carries no physical risk. Forum threads show disagreement about whether it is attractive, with some members arguing for masculine looks instead. As with any appearance goal, individual components such as aggressive dieting, drug use or surgery discussed in the same threads carry their own risks.

angle.text: It aims to change overall impression by working on the visible, adjustable parts of the face and body: body fat, skin, hair and grooming. Followers say the result looks friendly and youthful.

lead: Prettyboymaxxing is a looksmaxxing term for deliberately cultivating a soft, youthful, somewhat androgynous male appearance, often called the "prettyboy" look. Rather than building the heavy jaw, brow and muscle associated with the "chad" ideal, practitioners work on leanness, skin quality, hair and overall facial softness, aiming for a face and frame that read as friendly, clean and approachable.[1][2]

Posters on looksmax.org describe it as a stack of familiar softer techniques: leanmaxxing, skinmaxxing, hairmaxxing and fashionmaxxing, along with grooming changes such as shaving.[1][2] One widely read guide argues that prettyboys are "made" through these methods, while the masculine look depends more on bone structure.[1]

Looksmaxxing writers distinguish "softmaxxing" (skincare, grooming, clothing, fitness) from "hardmaxxing" (drugs, surgery).[3] Prettyboymaxxing sits mostly on the softmaxxing side, though some threads also compare it to surgical routes such as rhinoplasty and jaw surgery.[4] The look has parallels outside forums, such as the South Korean "kkonminam" (flower boy) style built around grooming, fashion and smooth skin.[5] No published research has evaluated prettyboymaxxing as a program.
infobox: Skincare, leaning down, hair, grooming, clothing

paras: The prettyboy look is described by its advocates as lean, smooth-skinned and soft-featured, with styled or longer hair and a friendly, approachable expression.[1] Forum posts say it appeals to younger audiences and social media in particular.[1]

A well-known thread frames the ideal differently, listing strong bone structure, good coloring, perfect skin, full lips, a lean muscular build and height as the aesthetic target, which shows that members hold varied pictures of the ideal.[6]

The aesthetic echoes older soft-masculine ideals. Wikipedia describes kkonminam as a South Korean term in use since the late 1990s for men focused on style, grooming and fashion, with imagery emphasising smooth, fair skin and silky hair, and traces its soft masculinity to the Japanese bishonen ideal in girls' manga.[5] Forum users do not usually cite these traditions, but the visual overlap is often noted by outside commentators.[5]

In general terms, forum members describe changes to body composition, skin, hair, grooming and clothing. One poster documenting eleven months of change listed shaving, a new hairstyle, getting rid of glasses, starting to lift and lean down to around 12% body fat, and better lighting in photos.[2]
Guides in the community carry titles such as an ultimate prettyboymaxxing guide and appealmaxxing guide.[7][8]

Members describe leaning down as a core step because lower body fat can sharpen facial contours and give a lighter frame; one poster reported reaching about 12% body fat while also starting to lift.[2]
Clear, even skin is the most repeated element in prettyboy guides, which connect it to skinmaxxing routines.[1][8]
Hairstyle changes, shaving, dropping glasses and fashion choices are listed as the quickest visible changes, with lighting and photo quality also acknowledged as factors.[1][2]

Supporters argue that the look gives more social ease and status among peers than hyper-masculine looks, and that it is achievable without surgery.[1] Critics in the same community argue that masculine features are more valued and that prettyboys are not seen as attractive by older women; those positions appear in replies to the same threads.[1][6]

Wikipedia's pretty privilege article collects studies linking perceived attractiveness with outcomes: a 2006 study by Mobius and Rosenblat found employers willing to offer attractive candidates about 10.5% higher salaries when other information was held constant, and a 2006 Wilson and Eckel study found attractive people were perceived as more trustworthy at first impression.[9] Edward Thorndike introduced the halo effect in a 1920 paper, describing how a favourable impression colours judgments of other traits.[9] These studies concern attractiveness in general and do not compare soft and masculine looks, so prettyboy-specific claims remain untested.

Prettyboymaxxing appears on looksmax.org in guides, progress threads and debate threads, including guides titled around "appealmaxxing" and "softmaxxing ascension".[1][2][7][8] Posters sometimes pit it against "mascmaxxing", arguing over which presentation wins attention; replies in these threads range from enthusiastic to dismissive.[1][6] Wikipedia notes that looksmaxxing spread to TikTok in the early 2020s, and that much press coverage has centred on its drug and surgery extremes.[3]

Writers on looksmaxxing generally describe skincare, grooming, clothing and fitness as the lower-intensity "softmaxxing" end of the practice.[3] No published human study has tested prettyboymaxxing or measured how the resulting look is perceived.

lore.intro: The term circulates on looksmax.org in guides, progress threads and debate threads, usually alongside skinmaxxing and leanmaxxing discussion.[1][2]

timeline.event: Edward Thorndike describes the halo effect, later used to explain why attractive people are judged favourably.[9]
The term kkonminam appears in South Korea for soft, groomed men as ads and dramas replace tough male imagery.[5]
Looksmaxxing terminology is coined on incel-linked forums, including the softmaxxing/hardmaxxing split.[3]
Looksmaxxing spreads to TikTok framed as self-improvement.[3]
